text: Clan Boyd is a Scottish clan from the Lowlands recognized by the Lord Lyon King of Arms. The name Boyd is derived from the Scottish Gaelic *buidh*, meaning fair or yellow, or possibly from *Bhoid*, the Gaelic name for the Isle of Bute, with the island's Gaelic name being *Eilean Bhòid* and the Marquess of Bute referred to as *Morair Bhoid*. The clan's progenitor is said to have been Robert, son of Simon and nephew of Walter fitz Alan, the first High Steward of Scotland, though genealogist William Anderson challenges this, arguing that Norman-origin dependents of the High Stewards would not use a Celtic nickname, and instead suggests Norman or Saxon origins. Historian George Fraser Black asserts that the first Boyds were vassals of the Norman de Morvilles, holding lands around Largs and Irvine, and that the surname may stem from the Gaelic for Bute. In 1205, Robert de Boyd (or Robertus de Boyd) witnessed a contract between the Lord of Eglinton and the burgh of Irvine, and Robert de Boyte appears on the Ragman Rolls in 1296, swearing homage to Edward I of England. The clan gained prominence at the Battle of Largs in 1263 when Robert Boyd was tasked with clearing Norsemen from Gold Berry Hill, a high ground overlooking the beach; King Alexander III uttered "Confido!" (I trust) as a royal gesture, which became the clan's motto and symbol. The name "Gold Berry" was later inscribed beneath the clan's early heraldic shield. In the 1290s, the Boyds allied with William Wallace during the Wars of Scottish Independence, and Duncan Boyd was executed in 1306 for supporting Scottish independence. Sir Robert Boyd, a probable grandson of the Largs-era Robert Boyd and a trusted commander of Wallace, supported King Robert the Bruce and fought at the Battle of Bannockburn in 1314, where the clan's Bannockburn Shield—a field of cobalt blue with a red and white checkerboard—originated. He was rewarded with lands previously confiscated from the Balliols, including Kilmarnock, Bodington, and other Ayrshire territories. Sir Thomas Boyd, 8th chief, killed Sir Alan Stewart of Darnley in a feud that was in its third year, and was subsequently killed in revenge by Alexander Stewart, brother of Alan, on 9 July 1439 at Craignaucht Hill, where Boyd's force of 100 men faced three detachments of 70 men each, resulting in a two-to-one numerical disadvantage. The battle was fierce, with both sides retreating and re-engaging upon hearing a trumpet, and ultimately ended in a Stewart victory. The feud continued, with another Stewart later killed by the Boyds in Dumbarton. The chief was raised to the peerage as Lord Boyd of Kilmarnock by James II of Scotland; upon James II's death, Robert Boyd, 1st Lord Boyd, became one of the regents for James III, and his younger brother served as the king's military tutor. Lord Boyd later held the office of Great Chamberlain, and his son Thomas married Princess Mary, the king's sister, and was granted the title Earl of Arran. The family's power attracted enemies, and in 1469, Lord Boyd, his son Thomas, and his brother Alexander were summoned to answer charges; Lord Boyd escaped to England, while Alexander was executed. Thomas, Earl of Arran, fled abroad and was well received in European royal courts. James Boyd, 2nd Lord Boyd and 11th chief, was killed in 1484 in a feud with Hugh Montgomerie, 1st Earl of Eglinton; he was succeeded by his uncle, Alexander Boyd, 3rd Lord Boyd and 12th chief, a favorite of James IV who became Bailie and Chamberlain of Kilmarnock. Alexander's son, Robert Boyd, 4th Lord Boyd, had his estates and honours restored by James V of Scotland in 1536 (though the Collins Scottish Clan & Family Encyclopedia attributes the restoration to Mary, Queen of Scots); Robert had two children, Robert and Margaret. Margaret married Neil Montgomery of Lainshaw, but the alliance was hostile, and in 1547, her father Robert Boyd, along with Mowat of Busbie, assassinated Neil Montgomery at Irvine in revenge for the death of his cousin James Boyd in 1484. A descendant of the first Lord Boyd received confirmation of the family's estates and honours from Mary, Queen of Scots, and after her escape from Lochleven, he joined her and fought at the Battle of Langside, making multiple visits to her while she was imprisoned in England; he died in 1590. During the Wars of the Three Kingdoms, Clan Boyd supported the royalist cause and was rewarded after the Restoration in 1660 when William, Lord Boyd, was created Earl of Kilmarnock. The third earl opposed the 1715 Jacobite rising and commanded Ayrshire volunteers for the government, but his son, the fourth earl, supported the 1745 rising, fighting for Charles Edward Stuart at Culloden, where he was made a member of the Privy Council and granted the rank of general. He was captured at Culloden, taken to the Tower of London, and beheaded on Tower Hill on 18 August 1746. All Boyd titles were forfeited, but his eldest son succeeded through his mother to the title of Earl of Erroll and changed his surname to Hay (see James Hay, 15th Earl of Erroll). The 22nd Earl of Erroll died in Kenya in 1941; his daughter was entitled to succeed to the earldom of Erroll and the chiefship of Clan Hay but was excluded from the barony of Kilmarnock, which could only pass to males. Consequently, the brother of the 22nd Earl resumed the surname Boyd and succeeded to the barony of Kilmarnock. Alastair Boyd, 7th Baron Kilmarnock and Chief of Clan Boyd, died on 19 March 2009; the barony and chiefship pass to his brother Dr. Robin Boyd, who has not yet claimed either title. The clan's coat of arms is quarterly: 1st Azure a fess chequy Argent and Gules (for Boyd), 2nd Argent three inescutcheons Gules (for Hay), 3rd Argent three gillyflowers Gules within a double tressure flory counter flory Vert (for Livingston), 4th Sable a bend between six billets Or (for Callendar). The crest badge, featuring a dexter hand erect in pale with outer fingers bowed inwards, bears the motto CONFIDO ("I trust") and is the heraldic property of the chief, though any clan member may wear it to show allegiance.
